# 1 Atomic Structure and Properties

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

At the foundation of chemistry lies atomic structure — the building blocks of
matter and how they are organised.

## Key definitions

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Atom** | The smallest unit of an element that maintains the chemical identity of that element. Atoms can be broken down further into subatomic particles, but doing so changes their fundamental properties |
| **Isotopes** | Variants of the same element containing the **same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons**, giving identical chemical properties but different masses |
| **Ion** | An atom or molecule that has gained or lost one or more electrons, resulting in a net positive or negative charge |
| **Atomic number ($Z$)** | The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which determines which element it is |
| **Mass number ($A$)** | The sum of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus |

Isotopes are the reason the first formula below is needed at all: because an
element occurs as several isotopes of different mass, its usable mass is an
average rather than a single value.

## Essential formulas

The **average atomic mass** of an element considers all its naturally occurring
isotopes and their relative abundances:

$$\text{Average atomic mass} = \sum(\text{isotopic mass} \times \text{fractional abundance})$$

**Worked example from the guide.** If an element has two isotopes of mass
$10.012$ amu (75%) and $11.009$ amu (25%):

$$(10.012 \times 0.75) + (11.009 \times 0.25) = 10.261\ \text{amu}$$

The relationship between mass number, atomic number and neutrons:

$$A = Z + N$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Atom** | The smallest unit of an element that maintains its chemical identity |
| **Isotopes** | Variants of an element with the same protons but different neutrons |
| **Ion** | An atom or molecule with a net charge from gaining or losing electrons |
| **Atomic number ($Z$)** | The number of protons, determining the element |
| **Mass number ($A$)** | The sum of protons and neutrons |
| **Average atomic mass** | The sum of each isotopic mass times its fractional abundance |

# 2 Molecular and Ionic Compound Structure

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Understanding how atoms combine into compounds is essential for predicting
chemical behaviour.

## Bond types

| Bond | Forms between | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Ionic** | Metals and nonmetals | **Complete transfer** of electrons; the resulting oppositely charged ions attract, forming a **crystalline lattice** |
| **Covalent** | Nonmetals | **Sharing of electron pairs**; polar or nonpolar depending on the electronegativity difference between the atoms |
| **Metallic** | Metal atoms | Valence electrons form a **sea of delocalised electrons**, allowing electrical conductivity and malleability |

Each bond's properties follow from its mechanism: a lattice of fixed ions is
rigid, whereas delocalised electrons are free to carry current.

## Alloys

**Alloys** are mixtures of metals, of two main types:

- **Interstitial alloys** have **smaller atoms fitting into the spaces between
  larger atoms** — carbon in steel
- **Substitutional alloys** have **atoms of similar size replacing each other** in
  the crystal structure — brass, which is copper and zinc

## Formula types

The **empirical formula** represents the **simplest whole-number ratio** of atoms
in a compound. The **molecular formula** shows the **actual number of atoms** of
each element in a molecule, and may be a multiple of the empirical formula.

## Essential formulas

Percent composition of an element in a compound:

$$\%\ \text{Composition} = \frac{\text{mass of element}}{\text{total molar mass}} \times 100\%$$

Molecular formula from the empirical formula:

$$\text{Molecular formula} = n \times \text{Empirical formula}, \qquad n = \frac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ionic bond** | A bond between metals and nonmetals through complete electron transfer, forming a crystalline lattice |
| **Covalent bond** | A bond between nonmetals through sharing electron pairs, polar or nonpolar by electronegativity difference |
| **Metallic bond** | A bond between metal atoms in which valence electrons form a sea of delocalised electrons |
| **Interstitial alloy** | An alloy whose smaller atoms fit into spaces between larger atoms, such as carbon in steel |
| **Substitutional alloy** | An alloy whose similarly sized atoms replace each other, such as brass |
| **Empirical formula** | The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound |
| **Molecular formula** | The actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule |

# 3 Intermolecular Forces and Properties

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Intermolecular forces (IMFs)** are the attractive forces **between** molecules,
influencing physical properties such as boiling point, melting point and
solubility. Unlike covalent or ionic bonds, which hold atoms together *within*
molecules, IMFs operate between separate molecules and are **generally much weaker
than chemical bonds**.

## The three forces, weakest first

**London dispersion forces** are the weakest type, **present in all molecules**.
They result from **temporary dipoles created by random electron movement**, and
their strength **increases with molecular size and surface area**. This is why
large nonpolar molecules like octane have higher boiling points than smaller
nonpolar ones like methane.

**Dipole–dipole interactions** occur between **polar molecules with permanent
dipoles**, the positive end of one attracted to the negative end of another. They
are **stronger than dispersion forces but weaker than hydrogen bonds**. Examples
include interactions between acetone molecules and between HCl molecules.

**Hydrogen bonding** is a special, particularly strong type of dipole–dipole
interaction, occurring when **hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative
element — N, O or F**. This creates a strong partial positive charge on the
hydrogen that can interact with lone pairs on nearby molecules. It is responsible
for **water's high boiling point** and unique properties.

## Impact on physical properties

The strength of intermolecular forces directly affects several properties, and all
four move together because all four depend on how hard it is to separate one
molecule from its neighbours.

| Property | Effect of stronger IMFs | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Boiling and melting points** | Increase | More energy is required to overcome the attractive forces |
| **Vapour pressure** | Decreases | Fewer molecules have enough energy to escape the liquid phase |
| **Viscosity** | Increases | Molecules have greater resistance to flowing past each other |
| **Surface tension** | Increases | Molecules at the surface are more strongly attracted to those in the liquid |

## Solubility

**Like dissolves like.** Polar substances tend to dissolve in polar solvents, and
nonpolar substances in nonpolar solvents. Dissolving requires **overcoming the
IMFs between solute particles and between solvent particles**, which is
energetically favourable when the solute–solvent interactions are **similar in
strength to the original interactions**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Intermolecular forces (IMFs)** | Attractive forces between molecules, generally much weaker than chemical bonds |
| **London dispersion forces** | The weakest IMF, present in all molecules, from temporary dipoles caused by random electron movement |
| **Dipole–dipole interactions** | Forces between polar molecules with permanent dipoles |
| **Hydrogen bonding** | A particularly strong dipole–dipole interaction where hydrogen bonds to N, O or F |
| **Vapour pressure** | The pressure that decreases as IMFs strengthen, as fewer molecules escape the liquid |
| **Viscosity** | Resistance to flow, increasing with stronger IMFs |
| **Surface tension** | The attraction of surface molecules to the liquid, increasing with stronger IMFs |
| **Like dissolves like** | The principle that polar dissolves in polar and nonpolar in nonpolar |

# 4 Chemical Reactions and Stoichiometry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Chemical reactions transform reactants into products through the **breaking and
forming of chemical bonds**.

## Types of reaction

| Type | General form |
|---|---|
| **Synthesis (combination)** | $A + B \rightarrow AB$ |
| **Decomposition** | $AB \rightarrow A + B$ |
| **Combustion** | $\text{Hydrocarbon} + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O$ |
| **Single replacement** | $A + BC \rightarrow AC + B$ |
| **Double replacement** | $AB + CD \rightarrow AD + CB$ |
| **Redox** | Involves electron transfer between species |

The **net ionic equation** shows only the species that **actually participate** in
the reaction, eliminating **spectator ions**, so that the representation focuses on
the chemical change that occurs.

## Stoichiometry

**Stoichiometry** is the calculation of reactants and products using the balanced
chemical equation. The **coefficients in a balanced equation represent the molar
ratios** of the substances involved.

Balancing an equation requires the **same number of atoms of each element on both
sides**, following the **law of conservation of mass**.

## The limiting reactant

The **limiting reactant** determines the **maximum amount of product** that can be
formed. It is the reactant **completely consumed** when the reaction reaches
completion.

To find it, **calculate the theoretical yield of product from each reactant**; the
reactant giving the **smallest** amount of product is limiting.

$$\text{Theoretical yield} = (\text{moles of limiting reactant}) \times (\text{stoichiometric ratio}) \times (\text{molar mass of product})$$

## Percent yield

Percent yield compares the actual product obtained to the theoretical amount
predicted by stoichiometry:

$$\%\ \text{Yield} = \frac{\text{Actual yield}}{\text{Theoretical yield}} \times 100\%$$

The order matters: the limiting reactant fixes the theoretical yield, and the
theoretical yield is what the actual yield is measured against.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Synthesis** | A combination reaction, $A + B \rightarrow AB$ |
| **Decomposition** | $AB \rightarrow A + B$ |
| **Combustion** | Hydrocarbon plus oxygen giving carbon dioxide and water |
| **Redox** | A reaction involving electron transfer between species |
| **Net ionic equation** | An equation showing only the participating species, eliminating spectator ions |
| **Spectator ions** | Ions that do not participate in the reaction |
| **Stoichiometry** | Calculating reactants and products using the balanced equation's molar ratios |
| **Limiting reactant** | The reactant completely consumed, determining the maximum product |
| **Theoretical yield** | The product predicted from the limiting reactant |
| **Percent yield** | Actual yield divided by theoretical yield, times 100% |

# 5 Kinetics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Chemical kinetics** is the study of **reaction rates** and the factors that
influence them, allowing chemists to control reaction speeds and determine
reaction mechanisms.

## Reaction rate

The **reaction rate** measures how quickly reactants are converted to products,
typically expressed as **change in concentration per unit time**.

Factors affecting reaction rates: **concentration, temperature, surface area,
catalysts, and the nature of the reactants**.

## Rate laws and reaction order

The **rate law** shows how reaction rate depends on reactant concentrations:

$$\text{Rate} = k[A]^m[B]^n$$

where $k$ is the **rate constant**, and $m$ and $n$ are the **reaction orders**
with respect to reactants $A$ and $B$. The **overall reaction order** is the sum of
the individual orders, $m + n$.

## Temperature and activation energy

Temperature affects reaction rates through the **Arrhenius equation**:

$$k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$$

where $E_a$ is the **activation energy**, $R$ the gas constant, $T$ the absolute
temperature and $A$ the **frequency factor**. Higher temperatures **increase the
proportion of molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier**.

## Half-life and integrated rate laws

| Order | Integrated rate law | Half-life |
|---|---|---|
| **First** | $[A] = [A]_0e^{-kt}$ | Constant: $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$ |
| **Second** | $1/[A] = 1/[A]_0 + kt$ | Depends on initial concentration |

The distinction is worth remembering as a pair: a first-order half-life is
independent of how much you start with, a second-order one is not.

## Reaction mechanisms

Most reactions occur through **a series of elementary steps** rather than a single
molecular collision; the **reaction mechanism** describes these steps. The
**slowest step — the rate-determining step — controls the overall reaction rate**.

The rate law can often **provide clues** about the mechanism, though additional
evidence is usually needed to confirm a proposed mechanism.

## Catalysts

**Catalysts increase reaction rates by providing an alternative reaction pathway
with a lower activation energy**, without being consumed. More molecular collisions
therefore result in successful reactions — but a catalyst **does not change the
overall energetics or the equilibrium position** of the reaction.

**Enzymes** are biological catalysts that can increase reaction rates by factors of
millions or more, through highly specific interactions with substrates.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chemical kinetics** | The study of reaction rates and the factors influencing them |
| **Reaction rate** | How quickly reactants become products, as change in concentration per unit time |
| **Rate law** | The expression showing how rate depends on reactant concentrations |
| **Rate constant ($k$)** | The constant in the rate law |
| **Reaction order** | The exponent on a reactant's concentration in the rate law; the overall order is their sum |
| **Arrhenius equation** | $k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, relating rate constant to temperature |
| **Activation energy ($E_a$)** | The energy barrier a reaction must overcome |
| **Frequency factor ($A$)** | The pre-exponential constant in the Arrhenius equation |
| **Reaction mechanism** | The series of elementary steps by which a reaction occurs |
| **Rate-determining step** | The slowest step in a mechanism, which controls the overall rate |
| **Catalyst** | A substance providing a lower-activation-energy pathway without being consumed, and without changing equilibrium |
| **Enzyme** | A biological catalyst acting through highly specific interactions with substrates |

# 6 Thermodynamics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Thermodynamics** is the study of energy transformations in chemical reactions and
physical processes. It allows us to **predict whether reactions will occur
spontaneously** and how much energy will be released or absorbed.

## The First Law

Energy **cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or converted** from one
form to another. In chemical systems we track energy changes through **enthalpy
($H$)**, the heat content of a system at constant pressure.

| Reaction | Heat | Sign of $\Delta H$ |
|---|---|---|
| **Endothermic** | Absorbs heat from its surroundings | Positive |
| **Exothermic** | Releases heat to its surroundings | Negative |

## Heat calculations

$$q = mc\Delta T$$

where $q$ is heat energy, $m$ is mass, $c$ is **specific heat capacity** and
$\Delta T$ the temperature change.

For enthalpy, using **standard enthalpies of formation**:

$$\Delta H = \sum \Delta H_{\text{products}} - \sum \Delta H_{\text{reactants}}$$

**Hess's Law** states that **enthalpy changes are additive**, allowing the enthalpy
change for a reaction to be calculated by breaking it into steps with known
enthalpies.

## The bond energy approach

$$\Delta H = \sum \text{Bonds broken} - \sum \text{Bonds formed}$$

**Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic); forming bonds releases energy
(exothermic).** That is why the subtraction runs in this direction.

## The Second Law and entropy

**Entropy ($S$)** measures **disorder or randomness** in a system. The Second Law
states that **the total entropy of the universe always increases for spontaneous
processes**.

Processes that **increase disorder** have positive $\Delta S$ — phase changes from
solid to liquid or liquid to gas, and reactions that increase the number of gas
molecules.

## Gibbs free energy

Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict spontaneity:

$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$

| $\Delta G$ | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negative** | Spontaneous process |
| **Positive** | Non-spontaneous process |
| **Zero** | At equilibrium |

The standard Gibbs free energy change relates to the equilibrium constant:

$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$$

This is the link between this topic and equilibrium: the same quantity that decides
spontaneity also fixes where the equilibrium sits.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Thermodynamics** | The study of energy transformations in reactions and physical processes |
| **First Law** | Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or converted |
| **Enthalpy ($H$)** | The heat content of a system at constant pressure |
| **Endothermic** | Absorbing heat from the surroundings; positive $\Delta H$ |
| **Exothermic** | Releasing heat to the surroundings; negative $\Delta H$ |
| **Specific heat capacity ($c$)** | The constant in $q = mc\Delta T$ |
| **Hess's Law** | Enthalpy changes are additive, so a reaction can be broken into steps of known enthalpy |
| **Entropy ($S$)** | A measure of disorder or randomness in a system |
| **Second Law** | The total entropy of the universe always increases for spontaneous processes |
| **Gibbs free energy ($G$)** | $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$; negative is spontaneous, zero is equilibrium |

# 7 Equilibrium

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Chemical equilibrium** occurs when the **rates of the forward and reverse
reactions become equal**, so that concentrations of reactants and products remain
constant.

## Dynamic equilibrium

Equilibrium is **dynamic**: reactions **continue to occur in both directions** even
though there is **no net change** in concentrations. This is different from a
static situation, where no reactions are occurring at all.

## The equilibrium constant

For a general reaction $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$:

$$K = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$$

where the brackets are **equilibrium concentrations** and the exponents are the
**stoichiometric coefficients** from the balanced equation.

The magnitude of $K$ indicates where the equilibrium position lies:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $K > 1$ | **Products favoured** — equilibrium lies to the right |
| $K < 1$ | **Reactants favoured** — equilibrium lies to the left |
| $K \approx 1$ | Significant amounts of **both** reactants and products present |

## The reaction quotient

The **reaction quotient ($Q$)** has the **same form as $K$** but uses
concentrations **at any point** in the reaction, not just at equilibrium.
Comparing $Q$ to $K$ predicts the direction of reaction:

| Comparison | Direction |
|---|---|
| $Q < K$ | Proceeds **forward**, toward products |
| $Q > K$ | Proceeds **in reverse**, toward reactants |
| $Q = K$ | The system is **at equilibrium** |

The system always moves so as to bring $Q$ towards $K$ — which is the same idea Le
Chatelier's Principle states qualitatively below.

**ICE tables** — Initial, Change, Equilibrium — are a systematic way to calculate
equilibrium concentrations, beginning by setting up a table with the initial
concentrations.

## Le Chatelier's Principle

When a system at equilibrium is **disturbed, the system will shift to counteract
the disturbance**.

| Change | Shift |
|---|---|
| **Adding reactants** | Toward products |
| **Adding products** | Toward reactants |
| **Decreasing volume (increasing pressure)**, for gas-phase reactions | Toward **fewer gas molecules** |
| **Increasing temperature**, endothermic reaction | Toward **products** |
| **Increasing temperature**, exothermic reaction | Toward **reactants** |
| **Catalyst** | **No change** in equilibrium position, but it is reached faster |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chemical equilibrium** | When forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and concentrations stay constant |
| **Dynamic equilibrium** | Equilibrium in which reactions continue in both directions with no net change |
| **Equilibrium constant ($K$)** | The ratio of product to reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient |
| **Reaction quotient ($Q$)** | The same expression as $K$ but at any point in the reaction |
| **ICE table** | An Initial, Change, Equilibrium table for calculating equilibrium concentrations |
| **Le Chatelier's Principle** | A disturbed equilibrium shifts to counteract the disturbance |

# 8 Acids and Bases

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three definitions

Each definition is broader than the one before it, which is why all three are
taught rather than only the most general.

| Definition | Acids | Bases | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Arrhenius** | Release $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions in water | Release $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions in water | Limited to aqueous solutions |
| **Brønsted–Lowry** | Proton ($\mathrm{H^+}$) donors | Proton acceptors | Applies to non-aqueous solutions; explains acid–base pairs |
| **Lewis** | Electron pair acceptors | Electron pair donors | The most general; explains reactions beyond traditional acid–base chemistry |

## Strong and weak

| | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Strong acids** | Completely dissociate in water | $\mathrm{HCl}$, $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{HBr}$, $\mathrm{HI}$, $\mathrm{HClO_4}$ |
| **Weak acids** | Partially dissociate in water | $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$, $\mathrm{HF}$, $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$ |
| **Strong bases** | Completely dissociate in water | $\mathrm{NaOH}$, $\mathrm{KOH}$, $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ |
| **Weak bases** | Partially dissociate in water | $\mathrm{NH_3}$, amines |

## Conjugate acid–base pairs

When an acid **donates** a proton it becomes its **conjugate base**; when a base
**accepts** a proton it becomes its **conjugate acid**.

**The strength of an acid is inversely related to the strength of its conjugate
base** — strong acids have weak conjugate bases, and vice versa.

## pH and pOH

$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^+}] \qquad \mathrm{pOH} = -\log[\mathrm{OH^-}] \qquad \mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14\ \text{(at 25\,°C)}$$

For **strong** acids and bases, $[\mathrm{H^+}]$ or $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ equals the
initial concentration of the acid or base — because dissociation is complete. For
**weak** acids and bases, equilibrium calculations using $K_a$ or $K_b$ are
necessary.

## Dissociation constants

For a weak acid $\mathrm{HA}$:

$$K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$$

For a weak base $\mathrm{B}$:

$$K_b = \frac{[\mathrm{BH^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}]}{[\mathrm{B}]}$$

The relationship between conjugate pairs:

$$K_a \times K_b = K_w = 1 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{(at 25\,°C)}$$

This is the quantitative form of the inverse relationship stated above: a larger
$K_a$ forces a smaller $K_b$.

## Buffers

**Buffers resist pH changes** when small amounts of acid or base are added. They
consist of a **weak acid and its conjugate base**, or a **weak base and its
conjugate acid**.

The **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation** relates buffer composition to pH:

$$\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\text{base}]}{[\text{acid}]}$$

**Buffer capacity is maximised when the ratio of base to acid is close to 1**,
which occurs when $\mathrm{pH} \approx \mathrm{p}K_a$ — as the equation shows,
since the log term is then zero.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Arrhenius definition** | Acids release $\mathrm{H^+}$ and bases release $\mathrm{OH^-}$ in water |
| **Brønsted–Lowry definition** | Acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors |
| **Lewis definition** | Acids are electron pair acceptors and bases are electron pair donors |
| **Strong acid** | An acid that completely dissociates in water |
| **Weak acid** | An acid that partially dissociates in water |
| **Conjugate base** | What an acid becomes after donating a proton |
| **Conjugate acid** | What a base becomes after accepting a proton |
| **pH** | $-\log[\mathrm{H^+}]$ |
| **pOH** | $-\log[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ |
| **$K_a$** | The acid dissociation constant |
| **$K_b$** | The base dissociation constant |
| **$K_w$** | The water constant, $1\times10^{-14}$ at 25 °C, equal to $K_a \times K_b$ |
| **Buffer** | A weak acid with its conjugate base (or weak base with conjugate acid) that resists pH change |
| **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation** | $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log([\text{base}]/[\text{acid}])$ |
| **Buffer capacity** | Maximised when the base-to-acid ratio is near 1, where $\mathrm{pH}\approx\mathrm{p}K_a$ |

# 9 Electrochemistry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Electrochemistry explores the relationship between **electricity and chemical
reactions** — essential for understanding batteries, corrosion and many industrial
processes involving electron transfer.

## Redox reactions

Electrochemistry centres on **redox (reduction–oxidation) reactions**, in which
electrons are transferred between species.

| Process | Electrons | Oxidation state |
|---|---|---|
| **Oxidation** | Loss of electrons | Increases |
| **Reduction** | Gain of electrons | Decreases |

**These always occur together** — one species is oxidised while another is
reduced. The species that **gets oxidised** is the **reducing agent** (reductant);
the species that **gets reduced** is the **oxidising agent** (oxidant).

That naming is the reverse of what it first suggests, and is worth fixing in mind:
the reducing agent is the one being oxidised.

## Electrochemical cells

| Cell | Reaction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Galvanic (voltaic)** | **Spontaneous** redox reactions that **produce** electricity | Batteries |
| **Electrolytic** | **Non-spontaneous** redox reactions **driven by** an external electrical source | Electroplating |

In both types:

- The **anode** is where **oxidation** occurs
- The **cathode** is where **reduction** occurs
- **Electrons flow from anode to cathode** in the external circuit
- **Anions move toward the anode** and **cations toward the cathode** in the electrolyte

## Cell potentials

The **standard cell potential** measures the electrical potential difference
between the two half-cells under standard conditions — **1 M, 1 atm, 25 °C**:

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$$

**Standard reduction potentials** are tabulated values allowing cell potentials to
be calculated for various combinations of half-reactions. **More positive $E^\circ$
values indicate stronger oxidising agents.**

## Relationship to thermodynamics

$$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}$$

where $n$ is the number of electrons transferred and $F$ is Faraday's constant,
$96{,}485$ C/mol.

| Cell potential | Free energy | Result |
|---|---|---|
| $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0$ | $\Delta G^\circ < 0$ | **Spontaneous** — galvanic cell |
| $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} < 0$ | $\Delta G^\circ > 0$ | **Non-spontaneous** — electrolytic cell |

## Non-standard conditions

The **Nernst equation** relates cell potential under non-standard conditions to the
standard cell potential:

$$E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q$$

where $Q$ is the reaction quotient. **At equilibrium $E = 0$ and $Q = K$**, giving:

$$E^\circ = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log K$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Oxidation** | Loss of electrons, increasing oxidation state |
| **Reduction** | Gain of electrons, decreasing oxidation state |
| **Reducing agent** | The species that gets oxidised |
| **Oxidising agent** | The species that gets reduced |
| **Galvanic (voltaic) cell** | A cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity |
| **Electrolytic cell** | A cell in which an external source drives a non-spontaneous reaction |
| **Anode** | Where oxidation occurs |
| **Cathode** | Where reduction occurs |
| **Standard cell potential** | $E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$, at 1 M, 1 atm and 25 °C |
| **Standard reduction potential** | A tabulated $E^\circ$; more positive values indicate stronger oxidising agents |
| **Faraday's constant ($F$)** | 96,485 C/mol |
| **Nernst equation** | $E = E^\circ - (0.0591/n)\log Q$, for non-standard conditions |

# 10 Laboratory Work and Measurement

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Titration

**Titration** is an analytical procedure used to **determine the concentration of
an analyte** by reacting it with a **standard solution of known concentration**. The
process begins by **placing a measured volume of the analyte solution in a flask**.

Two points must be distinguished:

- The **endpoint** is where the **indicator changes colour**, signalling that the
  titration should stop
- The **equivalence point** is where **stoichiometrically equivalent amounts** of
  analyte and titrant have reacted

The endpoint is an **observable approximation** of the equivalence point — the
thing you can see standing in for the thing you actually want.

## Concentration

**Molarity** is the most common way to express solution concentration:

$$\text{Molarity} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{litres of solution}}$$

When a solution is diluted, **the number of moles of solute remains constant**,
which is what the dilution equation expresses:

$$M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$$

Other concentration units:

| Unit | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Molality ($m$)** | Moles of solute per **kilogram of solvent** |
| **Mass percent** | (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100% |
| **Parts per million (ppm)** | (mass of solute / mass of solution) × $10^6$ |
| **Mole fraction ($X$)** | Moles of component / total moles of all components |

## Laboratory equipment

| Equipment | Use |
|---|---|
| **Analytical balance** | Measures mass precisely to 0.1 mg or better |
| **Volumetric flask** | Prepares solutions of precise volume and concentration |
| **Burette** | Delivers variable volumes with high precision (±0.02 mL) |
| **Pipette** | Transfers a precise volume of liquid |
| **Graduated cylinder** | Measures approximate volumes |

## Error analysis

All measurements contain some degree of error.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | How close a measurement is to the **true value** |
| **Precision** | How close **repeated measurements** are to each other |
| **Significant figures** | Indicate the precision of a measurement |

$$\%\ \text{Error} = \frac{\text{experimental value} - \text{accepted value}}{\text{accepted value}} \times 100\%$$

Accuracy and precision are independent: repeated measurements can agree closely
with one another and still all be wrong.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Titration** | Determining an analyte's concentration by reacting it with a standard solution of known concentration |
| **Analyte** | The substance whose concentration is being determined |
| **Endpoint** | Where the indicator changes colour, an observable approximation of the equivalence point |
| **Equivalence point** | Where stoichiometrically equivalent amounts of analyte and titrant have reacted |
| **Molarity ($M$)** | Moles of solute per litre of solution |
| **Molality ($m$)** | Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent |
| **Parts per million (ppm)** | Mass of solute over mass of solution, times $10^6$ |
| **Mole fraction ($X$)** | Moles of a component over total moles of all components |
| **Accuracy** | How close a measurement is to the true value |
| **Precision** | How close repeated measurements are to each other |
| **Percent error** | Experimental minus accepted, over accepted, times 100% |

# 11 Constants, Units and Exam Preparation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide notes that these values **will be provided on the equation sheet**, but
that knowing them **saves time during the test** and helps conceptual
understanding.

## Constants

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| **Gas constant ($R$)** | $0.0821$ L·atm/mol·K |
| **Gas constant ($R$)** | $8.314$ J/mol·K |
| **Avogadro's number** | $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$ |
| **Water constant ($K_w$) at 25 °C** | $1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ |
| **Faraday's constant** | $96{,}485$ C/mol e$^-$ |
| **Speed of light** | $3.00 \times 10^8$ m/s |
| **Planck's constant** | $6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s |

$R$ is listed twice because it has two commonly used values, and the units decide
which one applies.

## Standard conditions

- **Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP):** 273 K (0 °C) and 1 atm
- **Standard atmosphere:** 101.3 kPa or 760 mmHg
- **Standard molar volume of a gas at STP:** 22.4 L/mol

## Conversion factors

| Quantity | Equivalence |
|---|---|
| Pressure | 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.3 kPa |
| Volume | 1 L = 1000 mL = 1 dm³ |
| Energy | 1 cal = 4.184 J |
| Length | 1 Å = $1\times10^{-10}$ m = 100 pm |
| Temperature | 0 °C = 273.15 K |

## Common units

| Quantity | Units |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | joule (J), calorie (cal) |
| **Mass** | kilogram (kg), gram (g), milligram (mg) |
| **Length** | metre (m), centimetre (cm), nanometre (nm) |
| **Volume** | litre (L), millilitre (mL), cubic metre (m³) |
| **Pressure** | atmosphere (atm), pascal (Pa), torr, mmHg |
| **Time** | second (s), minute (min), hour (h) |
| **Temperature** | kelvin (K), celsius (°C) |
| **Amount** | mole (mol) |

## A problem-solving procedure

1. **Analyse the problem** — underline key information
2. **Select relevant formulas** — determine which equations apply
3. **Organise your work** — write each step clearly, **including units and
   conversion factors**
4. **Check your answer** — verify the units are correct and the result makes
   physical sense

Steps 3 and 4 work together: carrying units through the calculation is what makes
the final check possible.

## Self-care during exam preparation

The guide closes with five points: maintain a **balanced schedule** with regular
breaks; get **adequate sleep**, since sleep consolidates memory and improves
problem-solving; **stay physically active**, as exercise boosts brain function and
reduces stress; **eat well**, since nutrition supports cognitive function; and
**manage stress** with relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or meditation.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Gas constant ($R$)** | 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K, or 8.314 J/mol·K |
| **Avogadro's number** | $6.022\times10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$ |
| **STP** | Standard Temperature and Pressure: 273 K and 1 atm |
| **Standard molar volume** | 22.4 L/mol for a gas at STP |
| **Accuracy of a result** | Checked by confirming correct units and physical plausibility |
